label: fiction
title: The Clean Room
setting: In the present-day fictional city of Halen Ward, a research company leased a windowless suite above an otherwise ordinary commercial building. Independent refrigeration technician Nara Kelm was hired through a booking agency to service climate equipment in the outer plant corridor. Four months later, regulators opened the sealed inner room and found large-scale illegal drug manufacture. Nara now sits beside Soren Pell, accused of knowingly helping that manufacture continue.
charge: manufacturing a large commercial quantity of a controlled drug
elements: A large commercial quantity of a controlled drug was manufactured.
The accused knowingly took part in manufacturing that drug.
The accused intended the manufacturing activity to continue or succeed.
hook: Before every illegal run, the climate equipment changed. Nara's name appears on the screen, and she really did visit. Did a technician keep a hidden operation alive, or did that operation turn routine work into evidence against her?

accused.human: Nara Kelm, 39, runs a one-person refrigeration business. She usually accepts emergency work through booking agencies and records site visits on her phone. After taking time away to care for her brother, she was rebuilding her regular client list when this contract arrived.
accused.if_guilty: Any sentence is for the judge after the verdict. It must play no part in deciding whether the prosecution proved Nara's knowledge and intention.

prosecution.speaker: pc
prosecution.text: The sealed suite could not operate unless its air stayed within a narrow range. Nara wasn't a passer-by. Over four months she returned nine times at night, made changes shortly before production, questioned readings she knew were abnormal, accepted double her usual rate, and kept going. After the raid, she deleted the client's messages. You will hear competing explanations for the controller records. The prosecution asks you to judge those records within the full chronology, not in isolation, and decide when ordinary work became criminal participation.

defence.speaker: dc
defence.text: Nara's job began and ended at equipment outside an opaque, access-controlled room. Her client described confidential materials research and sent service tickets that looked ordinary. The records require careful separation: a name displayed on a screen is not necessarily the signed identity of the device underneath it. Rian Vesk brings useful evidence and a reason to help himself. The defence doesn't say Nara asked every question she should have. It says carelessness and suspicion aren't knowing manufacture. Listen for what each fact actually proves.

prosecution.speaker: pc
prosecution.text: The machine-identity evidence matters, and the prosecution doesn't ask you to ignore it: eighteen commands came from an internal controller. But that correction doesn't erase the nine adjustments Nara really made, the warning in her own words, the premium payments, two further visits, or her deletion after the raid. A research story may explain how she entered the arrangement. You may conclude that the accumulating signs later made the criminal purpose plain enough, and that she deliberately kept the manufacture running.

defence.speaker: dc
defence.text: Start by correcting the loudest accusation. The screen put Nara's name beside eighteen commands; the authenticated, signed records put every one on an internal controller available to the operators. What remains is a contractor making nine ordinary-range adjustments after plausible tickets, from outside a room she couldn't see. Her questions, extra pay, and panicked deletion are legitimate concerns. They support a suspicious reading, but also an innocent one. If both remain reasonably possible, knowledge and intention haven't been proved. That is reasonable doubt.

epilogue: After the trial, the sealed suite remained closed while separate proceedings concerning its operators continued. The regulator changed its reports so a displayed account name appeared beside, not instead of, the signed device identity. Rian Vesk still faced sentence for his own conduct. Nara returned to refrigeration work under contracts requiring a named safety contact and written reasons for restricted access. None of those later steps answered what she had known during the charged months.

beats.speaker: pc
beats.text: The parties provide an agreed chronology and floor plan. A research company leased the sealed suite in early spring. A booking agency engaged Nara to maintain the external climate equipment. She attended nine alarm calls over four months but had no pass for the inner room. Police opened that room after the final visit. The plan marks the corridor panel where Nara worked, the opaque inner door, and the separate controller later found inside.
beats.reveal_note: The neutral chronology and plan orient the jury. They prove Nara's repeated proximity but also the physical boundary around her work.

beats.speaker: judge
beats.text: Knowledge means awareness of the essential criminal activity; Nara need not have known the drug's exact chemical name. Intention means that she meant her work to help the manufacture continue or succeed, not merely that it did help. Both may be proved by reasonable inference, without a confession. Before finding guilt by inference, however, guilt must be the only reasonable conclusion from the evidence as a whole. Nara need not prove the research explanation was true. If, after considering all the evidence, you are not sure the prosecution proved every element beyond reasonable doubt, your verdict must be Not Guilty. Do not research this case or seek outside information.
beats.reveal_note: The direction keeps the inquiry on knowledge and intention and states the reasonable-doubt standard without reducing it to any imaginable doubt.

twist: The authors' reference resolution is Not Guilty. The authenticated machine-identity records show that an internal suite controller—not Nara's handset—issued the eighteen commands carrying her displayed account name, while restricted access and the research cover story leave a reasonable possibility that her nine real visits were unwitting. The strongest prosecution interpretation remains substantial: Nara recognised abnormal demand, returned twice, accepted premium pay, and deleted messages after the raid. Those facts support suspicion, but do not prove beyond reasonable doubt that she knew about controlled-drug manufacture.

jurors.label: Juror 2 — Anya
jurors.persona: Anya starts with the name on the screen, then asks whether anyone has separated Nara's real work from the added commands.

agree: Eighteen commands under her name—how am I meant to ignore that?
pushback: Wait, are we mixing up the nine real visits and the eighteen other commands?
concede: All right. Her name was on the screen, but her handset didn't send those eighteen commands.
burden_drift: She kept going back. Shouldn't she have to explain every visit?
burden_correct: No, I've got that backwards. The Crown has to prove what she knew.
final: The screen has been corrected. For me, the nine real visits are the question now.

jurors.label: Juror 3 — Bram
jurors.persona: Bram finds repeated night visits hard to explain and keeps testing how much the restricted corridor really concealed.

agree: Once is a callout. Nine night visits before nine runs? That's a pattern.
pushback: But what could she actually see from that corridor? Nothing, apparently.
concede: The routine tickets and the research story could keep a contractor outside the real business.
burden_drift: If it was innocent, why didn't she walk away when the alarms looked wrong?
burden_correct: That's a fair question, but it isn't her burden to solve it.
final: I don't like her choices. I have to decide what they prove she knew.

jurors.label: Juror 4 — Cel
jurors.persona: Cel slows the room down whenever assistance, suspicion, and knowledge begin to blur together.

agree: Can we name the step we're taking? Her work helped. That doesn't tell us what she knew.
pushback: Suspicion of secrecy isn't automatically knowledge of controlled-drug manufacture.
concede: The signed device source removes the screen's strongest accusation. We have to reassess the rest.
burden_drift: The scale of this operation makes an innocent explanation feel uncomfortable.
burden_correct: Uncomfortable isn't the standard. Has the Crown excluded unwitting maintenance?
final: My verdict turns on whether unwitting maintenance remains a reasonable possibility.

jurors.label: Juror 5 — Dev
jurors.persona: Dev is persuaded by concrete records but gets impatient when either side asks a technical exhibit to answer a human question.

agree: The timing is hard to brush off. Those changes landed exactly when the suite needed them.
pushback: Which part is fixed: the name we can edit, or the signed device record?
concede: That changes it for me. The dramatic eighteen-command trail came from inside the suite.
burden_drift: She understands these systems, so surely she'd know what the pattern meant.
burden_correct: Actually, expertise explains the repair. It doesn't identify the hidden product.
final: I won't ask the device signature to decide more than the source of those commands.

jurors.label: Juror 6 — Esra
jurors.persona: Esra keeps the discussion moving by asking each speaker which disputed element a fact actually bears on.

agree: We're all agreed the manufacture happened. Which fact proves Nara knew that?
pushback: One at a time—are we arguing assistance, knowledge, or intention?
concede: The device signature doesn't answer everything, but it takes eighteen supposed acts off Nara's side of the ledger.
burden_drift: Because the operation was serious, I keep wanting a completely innocent explanation.
burden_correct: Let's reset. We don't need to approve of her conduct; the Crown must prove the elements.
final: I've kept assistance, knowledge, and intention separate. That's how I'll decide.

jurors.label: Juror 7 — Fenn
jurors.persona: Fenn distrusts premium payments and polished excuses, yet will change course when another juror gives the money an ordinary explanation.

agree: Double money, after dark, no site name. That sounds like hush money to me.
pushback: Maybe. But isn't double rate also exactly what an emergency contractor charges at night?
concede: The agency contract gives the payment a normal explanation. I can't just choose the nastier one.
burden_drift: She took the money, so why shouldn't she prove it was clean?
burden_correct: No—Dara Venn has to prove what Nara understood the money was for.
final: I have to decide what the payment meant, not just how it looks.

jurors.label: Juror 8 — Gio
jurors.persona: Gio initially trusts the tidy controller history, then focuses on exactly what its authenticated fields can and cannot show.

agree: On the first screen, I read the label as attribution. I suspect most of us did.
pushback: But the examiner said that field is editable. Why would we rank it above the signed source?
concede: The copies and signatures check out. Those eighteen commands came from an internal controller.
burden_drift: Nara's name is real, so part of me wants her to prove how it was copied.
burden_correct: The Crown tendered the source record. We don't have to guess who altered the label to use it properly.
final: Whatever my verdict, it will use the signed source rather than the visible label.

jurors.label: Juror 9 — Hale
jurors.persona: Hale listens closely for what Rian admits against his own interest and what he may be saying to improve his position.

agree: Rian's account of the seventh visit matches Nara's own message. That's hard to dismiss.
pushback: He can remember the cover story and still be guessing about Nara's mind.
concede: His account cuts both ways: she asked a sharp question, but the manager answered with the same research story.
burden_drift: Rian admitted the crime, and I catch myself asking Nara to prove she was different.
burden_correct: That's not fair. His guilt can't fill the gap in proof about her knowledge.
final: I've separated what Rian personally heard from what he hopes or assumes.

jurors.label: Juror 10 — Iri
jurors.persona: Iri keeps returning to the deleted messages and needs the room to distinguish later panic from earlier knowledge.

agree: Why delete the messages if she had nothing to hide? I can't get past that.
pushback: Hold on. The deletion came after the raid told her what the site was. Timing matters.
concede: I accept that panic is possible, especially once the accusing account label appeared.
burden_drift: Still, she deleted them. Doesn't she owe us a convincing innocent reason?
burden_correct: No. Her explanation can be weak and the prosecution can still fall short on earlier knowledge.
final: I've placed the deletion after the raid and decided how much that timing matters.

jurors.label: Juror 11 — Joss
jurors.persona: Joss thinks aloud, sometimes confuses benefit with intent, and corrects course when another juror separates the two.

agree: I'm stuck on this: the manufacture needed her adjustments, so doesn't that make her part of it?
pushback: No, sorry—that proves the work helped. It doesn't prove she understood why.
concede: The routine tickets show how real repairs could feed a hidden operation without the technician seeing it.
burden_drift: Because her work mattered so much, I keep wanting her to prove ignorance.
burden_correct: But knowledge is an element. The prosecution has to prove it.

jurors.label: Juror 12 — Kemi
jurors.persona: Kemi tests both narratives against the same record and resists letting a clean interface settle a messy question.

agree: The account name and timing make a neat guilt story. I can see why the Crown starts there.
pushback: The device signature doesn't prove innocence. It does prove the first screen blamed the wrong device.
concede: So we remove eighteen commands, keep nine real visits, and ask what those nine prove.
burden_drift: Do we need Nara to show she never agreed to lend her account name?
burden_correct: No. The signed source already shows where those commands originated.
final: After correcting the record, I'll decide what the remaining conduct proves.
